message:
Please review the following document.

<document>
**MEMO**

**To:** Director of Procurement, Halvorsen Controls
**From:** Strategic Sourcing
**Date:** November 13, 2026
**Re:** Supplier recommendation for the T-series thermostat housing

**Recommendation**

Award the T-series housing to Supplier A (Ohio) on a 12-month contract starting March 2027, with an option to extend to the mid-2028 redesign. Do not split volume with Supplier B now. Instead, invite B to quote on the redesigned housing once the February tariff decision is known.

**Why B cannot be the sole supplier**

Brightline Homes buys about 35% of T-series volume. Its contract requires USMCA regional content, and a housing made in Vietnam fails that rule. Using B for everything would put that contract at risk. The real choice is between two options:

- A for all volume, or
- A for Brightline's units and B for the rest.

**All-in cost per unit**

| | Supplier A | Supplier B |
|---|---|---|
| Price | $3.40 | $2.55 |
| Freight and duty | n/a | $0.38 |
| Rework (defect rate × $14) | $0.06 | $0.25 |
| Carrying cost of 8 extra weeks of safety stock | n/a | $0.09 |
| Tooling spread over 18 months | $0.19 | $0.09 |
| **Total** | **$3.65** | **$3.36** |
| **Total with the proposed 25% tariff** | **$3.65** | **$4.00** |

I planned on 300,000 units a year rather than the 400,000 forecast. Actual volumes fell 26–29% short of forecast in each of the last two years.

**Split sourcing barely pays off**

B could supply at most 65% of volume, about 290,000 units over 18 months. Leaving tooling aside, B costs $0.18 less per unit than A, which saves about $54,000. B's $40,000 tooling cost brings the net saving down to roughly $14,000 over the life of the program. Even if the 400,000 forecast holds, the net saving is only about $32,000.

That small saving carries three risks.

- **Tariff.** A 25% tariff on B's $2.55 declared value adds $0.64 per unit. B would then cost about $0.45 more than A on every unit, or roughly $90,000 a year. We would have to sign B's 12-month minimum in December, before the February decision is known.
- **Quality.** B's defect rate is 4.5 times A's. My $14 rework figure assumes every defect is caught at final assembly. One defect reaching customers could erase the saving many times over. The 2023 recalls cost $410,000. They came from a different supplier, so they are not evidence against B, but they show what a field failure costs. B's offer to host one of our quality engineers would help during the ramp-up, not afterward.
- **Responsiveness.** With an 11-week lead time, we would be slow to adjust when volumes miss forecast, which has happened in each of the last two years. Running two suppliers would also mean two sets of tooling and more work to manage.

**The CFO's 10% target**

Choosing a housing supplier will not reach the 10% COGS reduction. Even sourcing everything from B, which we cannot do, would cut housing cost by only about 8%. The housing is one part of total T-series COGS. Better ways to pursue the target:

- Negotiate A's price using a realistic 300,000-unit commitment and a term that runs to the redesign.
- Ask A to lower or spread out its $85,000 tooling charge.
- Set a cost target for the 2028 redesign and open the new tooling to competitive bids, including B and Mexican molders.

**Next steps**

Request A's best-and-final offer at 300,000 units by December 5. Order tooling by mid-December.

---

###
</document>

It was written from this brief:

<brief>
Write a vendor recommendation memo (about 450-550 words) to the Director of Procurement at Halvorsen Controls, choosing between two suppliers for the plastic housing used in its thermostat product line. The director needs a recommendation she can take to the CFO before tooling is ordered in December.

Halvorsen needs a supplier for the injection-molded housing for its T-series thermostats. Sales forecasts 400,000 units for 2027. Over the last two years, actual volumes were 310,000 (against a forecast of 420,000) and 290,000 (against a forecast of 410,000). Supplier A (Ohio): $3.40 per unit, 0.4% defect rate, 3-week lead time, one-time tooling cost of $85,000. Supplier B (Vietnam): $2.55 per unit, plus about $0.38 per unit in freight and duty, 1.8% defect rate, 11-week lead time, one-time tooling cost of $40,000. A defective housing is usually found at final assembly. Rework, including scrapped parts and labor, costs about $14 per defective unit. Because of B's longer lead time, operations estimates Halvorsen would need to hold about 8 more weeks of safety stock. Inventory carrying cost is 20% a year. Halvorsen's largest customer, Brightline Homes, buys about 35% of T-series volume. Brightline's contract, renewed last spring, requires that products meet USMCA regional-content rules, which the plastic housing would not meet if made in Vietnam. The government is reviewing tariffs on this category of products from Vietnam and is expected to decide in February 2027. One option under consideration is an additional 25% tariff on the declared value of the part. Engineering plans a redesign of the T-series for mid-2028 that will need new tooling, so tooling bought now will be used for about 18 months. The CFO has asked for a 10% reduction in the cost of goods sold for the T-series. The Quality Manager opposes Supplier B. She points to two field-failure recalls in 2023 that came from a different offshore supplier and cost Halvorsen $410,000. Supplier B has offered to pay for one of Halvorsen's quality engineers to spend a month at its plant during the production ramp-up. Both suppliers can start production by March 2027. Neither will accept a contract shorter than 12 months.
</brief>

Its author expects a reviewer to raise:

<expected>
1. **Volume basis.** Using 300,000 units instead of the official forecast is a judgment call that Sales may dispute. The memo should show the result at both volumes side by side.
2. **Tooling life.** Production runs from March 2027 to mid-2028, which is about 15–16 months, not 18. Using 18 months understates tooling cost per unit, and the shorter period would hurt A more than B.
3. **Inventory carrying cost.** The figure covers only the extra safety stock. It ignores the roughly 11 weeks of goods in transit, which Halvorsen may own depending on shipping terms. Including that would raise B's cost.
4. **Tariff probability.** The memo treats the 25% tariff as a reason to wait but never estimates how likely it is or calculates an expected cost.
5. **Tariff base.** The memo assumes "declared value" means $2.55. It does not check whether the $0.38 for freight and duty already includes some tariff.
6. **Field-failure risk.** The quality risk is described but not quantified. There is no estimate of how many defects reach customers for either supplier. Mentioning the 2023 recalls may also seem to lend weight to the Quality Manager's view, which the memo admits is not about B.
7. **A's escaped defects.** A's 0.4% defect rate also carries some field-failure risk, and the memo ignores it.
8. **Unsupported claim about COGS.** The memo says housing is "one part of COGS" without stating total T-series COGS. Its conclusion about the 10% target is reasonable but not shown with numbers.
9. **No negotiation targets.** The memo recommends negotiating with A but gives no target price or evidence that A has room to move.
10. **Value of a second supplier undersold.** Having two suppliers protects against a disruption at A, and the memo does not price that benefit.
11. **Brightline details.** The memo does not quantify the cost of breaching Brightline's contract. It also does not check whether Brightline's units could be kept separate from other units in production, which split sourcing would require.
12. **Missing options.** The memo does not consider other suppliers (for example, in Mexico) or a B contract that depends on the tariff outcome.
13. **Rounding.** Per-unit figures are rounded, so the totals do not exactly match the line items.
</expected>
response:
# Review: T-series housing supplier memo

**Verdict:** The memo is sound and nearly ready to send. The recommendation follows from the numbers, the arithmetic checks out, and the Brightline constraint is used well to narrow the choice. The main fix is the tooling period. Correcting it makes the case for A stronger, so it's worth doing before this goes to the CFO.

## Arithmetic check

I recomputed every figure from the brief.

| Item | Memo | Recomputed | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rework A / B | $0.06 / $0.25 | $0.056 / $0.252 | ✓ |
| Carrying cost (8/52 × 20% × $2.93 landed) | $0.09 | $0.090 | ✓ |
| Tooling A / B (450k units) | $0.19 / $0.09 | $0.189 / $0.089 | ✓ |
| Totals | $3.65 / $3.36 | $3.645 / $3.361 | ✓ |
| Tariff (25% × $2.55) | $0.64 → $4.00 | $0.6375 → $3.999 | ✓ |
| Gap excluding tooling | $0.18 | $0.184 | ✓ (the rounded lines give $0.19) |
| Split saving at 300k / 400k | $14k / $32k | $13.8k / $31.8k | ✓ |
| Post-tariff gap, per year | $0.45, ~$90k | $0.454 × 195k = $88.5k | ✓ |
| Forecast misses | 26–29% | 26.2% / 29.3% | ✓ |
| Defect ratio | 4.5× | 1.8 / 0.4 = 4.5 | ✓ |
| Housing cost cut if all B | ~8% | 7.9% | ✓ |

## Issues not on your expected list

1. **The tooling correction nearly wipes out the split saving.** Your item 2 is right, but its biggest effect isn't on the table. At 15–16 months, B's share is about 245,000–260,000 units. That gives gross savings of $45,000–48,000, so the **net saving falls to about $5,000–8,000**. This is the strongest single number for the recommendation, and the memo should use it.
2. **A's price under a split may not hold.** The $3.40 was presumably quoted for full volume. If A supplies only Brightline's 35%, it may reprice upward, which would erode the split saving further.
3. **The tariff row leaves carrying cost unchanged.** A higher landed value raises carrying cost from about $0.09 to $0.11. This is small, but it understates B's cost, and it's separate from the in-transit point in your item 3.
4. **The "8%" comparison is misleading.** Putting "8% of housing cost" next to a "10% of COGS" target makes them sound almost comparable. The real point is that housing is a small share of COGS, so 8% of it is a fraction of a percent of COGS. This overlaps with your item 8, but the framing itself needs fixing, not just the missing COGS figure.
5. **Tooling is counted twice in the narrative.** The Responsiveness bullet cites "two sets of tooling" as a risk, but B's $40,000 is already deducted in the split math.
6. **"Sign B's 12-month minimum in December" goes beyond the brief.** The brief says neither supplier accepts a contract shorter than 12 months and that tooling is ordered in December. That supports the timing argument, but the memo should present it as an inference rather than a fact.
7. **B's quality-engineer offer is understated.** "Host" undersells it: B offered to *pay* for the engineer's month on site.
8. **Next-steps timing is tight.** BAFO is due December 5 and tooling must be ordered by mid-December. That leaves little room to negotiate the tooling charge, which the memo also recommends.
9. **Form issues:**
   - The memo appears to run about 580–620 words, above the 450–550 target.
   - "I planned" is first person in a memo signed by "Strategic Sourcing."
   - A stray `---` / `###` sits at the end of the document.

## Comments on your expected list

- **Item 13 (rounding) is mostly wrong as stated.** The table totals do match their line items. The only mismatch is the $0.18 gap in the text versus $0.19 from the rounded table lines. A footnote would cover it.
- **Item 1 is already half addressed.** The split section gives both volumes ($14k and $32k). Only the main table lacks a 400k column.
- **Item 2:** see point 1 above. It matters more than the expected list suggests.
- **Item 7 is fair but low priority.** Counting A's escaped defects symmetrically would likely widen the gap in A's favor, since B escapes 4.5× as many.
- **Items 4, 5, 10, 11, and 12 are the substantive gaps:**
  - tariff probability and expected cost
  - what the tariff is charged on
  - the value of having a second supplier
  - Brightline breach cost and whether its units can be kept separate
  - a tariff-contingent B contract or a Mexican molder
  
  Any of these could come up when the CFO pushes back. A sentence each would close most of them.

## Suggested priority

1. Fix the tooling period and report the reduced split saving.
2. Reframe the 8% versus 10% comparison.
3. Add a line on tariff likelihood and a contingent-contract option.
4. Trim to length and clean up the form issues.
